index.t055: 57 of 61 months are profitable. Four are negative: January 2022 (−6.8%), January 2023 (−5.0%), February 2024 (−0.1%) and August 2024 (−10.2%), the worst month on record. The best month was March 2026, +44.6%. The average across all months is +16.0%.
index.t060: Separately, Algorithm 2 drew down 19.4% and Algorithm 1 7.8%, summing to 27.2%. The portfolio drawdown is 16.3%: risk is dampened because the algorithms lose on different days. This is measured, not asserted — across 600 days of joint trading both were negative 150 times against 149 expected by chance.
index.t062: Everything shown above is calculated on balance — on closed trades. But while a position is open the account fluctuates, and the screen shows a different figure — equity, the funds together with the floating result. Its drawdown is deeper, and it is equity that you will see in your own account.
index.a187: Drawdown on balance and on equity
index.t065: On closed trades the account drew down 16.3%, on equity — 21.2%: deeper by a factor of 1.30. Sampling is hourly, 39,000–41,000 readings per source.
index.t067: The equity drawdown is 4.9% deeper than the balance one — the gap between 21.2% and 16.3%. You would expect a floating loss to explain it: open positions go negative, the account sinks further. But over five years the floating loss never once exceeded 2.2% of the deposit — half of what would be needed. So where does the rest come from? Let us take apart the worst episode.
index.t074: Here is the answer: the depth came not from a floating loss, but from floating profit at the moment of the peak. In July the account stood at 584% on closed trades, and open positions showed a further +6.2%. The terminal read 590% — but those six percent were on the screen, not in the pocket. Then the balance fell by 14.6%, the unrealised profit evaporated, and from its high the account came down to 569%.
index.t076:
This is the whole gap between the two curves: above zero the open positions
  are in profit, below zero at a loss.
index.t077: 83% of the time the floating result is non-negative — positions are either in profit or closed. The upward peaks run far higher than the dips: up to +10.4% against −2.2%. It is exactly this asymmetry that creates inflated highs, from which the drawdown is then measured.
index.t078: Hence the practical conclusion. On a good day the figure in the terminal is inflated by unrealised profit, and when that goes it feels as though more has been lost than really was. Knowing this quantity matters so you are not frightened in the moment. And the control thresholds are set on balance: the watcher measures a hundred closed trades, and the alarm must trigger on the same thing that is being measured.
index.t080: History happened to run in one particular order of trades. To see how much the result depends on that order, we shuffled it 20,000 times and looked at what came out.
index.t081: How the account might have gone
index.t082:
The same 3,801 trades arranged in a different order. In red — what actually
  happened; dashed — the median of all variants.
index.t087: The ends converge for a reason: shuffling changes the order but not the set of trades, so every variant finishes at the same total. The spread lives in the middle of the road — and it is moderate: against an actual +478% at the halfway mark, the simulated variants fall within a corridor from +400% to +573%.
index.t088: For drawdown the reference point is this: a median of 23%, and that is what you should plan around. A drawdown deeper than 30% appeared in 12% of the recalculations, deeper than 40% — in 1.2%. The actual 16.3% turned out milder than in 98% of variants.
index.t089: The order was shuffled in two ways: by whole trading days (1,204 days) and by individual trades (3,801 trades). The first preserves the fact that on a given day several instruments often sink together; the second destroys that link but gives four times as many steps. The estimates differ by about one percent — so the figure is not an artefact of the method but a property of the strategy itself.
index.t090: How to read the table. On the left is the drawdown level in percent of the deposit; in the middle, the share out of twenty thousand recalculations where the account went deeper; on the right, how long such a drawdown lasted. Deeper than 40% went 240 variants out of twenty thousand, deeper than 50% — twenty-four, deeper than 60% — four. The last row is empty for a reason: not one of the twenty thousand variants went deeper than 70%, the heaviest reached 69.2%.
